sections.markdown:
## C — Driving safely, part one: tire checks, sign colors and shapes, stop and yield rules, emergency vehicles, traffic and arrow signals, turns on red, pedestrian signals, lane markings, center turn lanes, railroad crossings and school zones
Knowledge domain: the traffic-control language a Nevada driver must read instantly — what each sign color and shape means, how to handle stop and yield signs, every steady, flashing and arrow signal, pedestrian signals, white and yellow pavement lines, center turn lanes, railroad crossings and school-zone limits.

FACT_ID: sec04-F01 | anchor: A01
Check tire pressure with a gauge before getting in, using the recommended psi from the owner's manual or the driver's side door jamb, and adjust it if needed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec04-F02 | anchor: A01
Inspect tires for wear and damage once a month or before a long trip; in the penny test, if tread covers any part of Lincoln's head placed in the shallowest groove, the tread depth is safe, and less tread sharply cuts grip in bad conditions. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec04-F03 | anchor: A02
Signs serve three purposes, to regulate, to warn and to inform, and their shapes and colors carry set meanings so the message is read quickly. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec04-F04 | anchor: A02
Sign colors: red means stop, no or do not; green gives direction or guidance; yellow or yellow-green is a general warning; white marks a regulation, law or rule. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec04-F05 | anchor: A02
Sign colors: orange warns of road construction or repair, blue points to driver services such as food and lodging, and brown marks recreation and scenic information. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec04-F06 | anchor: A02
Sign shapes: an eight-sided octagon means stop, a diamond means warning, a rectangle gives regulations or directions, and an inverted triangle means yield right-of-way. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec04-F07 | anchor: A02
Sign shapes: a pennant means no passing, a five-sided pentagon marks school zones and crossings, a circle warns of a railroad crossing ahead, a crossbuck marks the crossing itself and a shield is a route marker. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec04-F08 | anchor: A03
At a stop sign, stop completely behind the crosswalk or stop line, and if the cross street is hidden, ease forward slowly until you can tell it is safe. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-F09 | anchor: A03
Where no stop line or crosswalk exists, slow and stop if needed at the point closest to the intersection that gives a view of oncoming through traffic, then yield to pedestrians and cross traffic before going. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-F10 | anchor: A03
At a four-way stop, wait for vehicles already in the intersection and let vehicles that arrived before you go first. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-F11 | anchor: A03
A yield sign works like a stop sign except you may keep moving without a full stop when it is safe; slow down and yield to pedestrians, through traffic, drivers already on the highway and vehicles making a U-turn. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-F12 | anchor: A03
When a police car, fire engine, ambulance or other emergency vehicle approaches with its siren and red lights on, pull to the right edge and stop until it has passed, but never stop inside an intersection. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-F13 | anchor: A03
Regulatory signs are rectangles with a white background and must be obeyed; warning signs are yellow diamonds with black letters or symbols that signal hazards ahead. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-F14 | anchor: A03
Railroad crossing signs warn you to slow and possibly stop; look both ways and stay off the tracks whenever a train is approaching. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-F15 | anchor: A04
Most work-area signs are diamond-shaped; drivers must slow down and obey posted signs and any flaggers, and violations in work zones carry increased fines. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F16 | anchor: A04
When traffic lights are out, come to a full stop, yield to pedestrians and to vehicles already stopped or in the intersection, then proceed with caution. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F17 | anchor: A04
At a red light, stop completely behind the crosswalk or stop line, or before entering the intersection if neither exists, and stay stopped until the light turns green. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F18 | anchor: A04
Unless a sign prohibits it, you may turn right on red after a complete stop, signalling first and waiting until vehicles and pedestrians are clear. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F19 | anchor: A04
A steady yellow light warns that red is coming: stop if you have not entered the intersection, keep going and clear it if you already have, and never speed up to beat the light. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F20 | anchor: A04
A green light allows going straight, turning right or turning left unless a sign forbids the turn. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F21 | anchor: A04
A flashing red light means a full stop and going only when the road is clear and you have the right-of-way, exactly like a stop sign, while a flashing yellow light means proceed with caution. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F22 | anchor: A04
A red arrow forbids the movement it points to, and drivers facing it must stop unless they are entering for a movement another signal allows. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F23 | anchor: A04
A steady yellow arrow warns that the arrow is about to turn red and you should clear the intersection; a flashing yellow arrow lets you turn after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F24 | anchor: A04
A green arrow lets you go the way it points and protects the turn from other traffic, yet you must still yield to pedestrians, bicycles and vehicles already in the intersection. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F25 | anchor: A04
A left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street whose traffic flows to the left, after signalling, stopping fully and yielding, unless a sign, arrow or officer forbids it. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec04-F26 | anchor: A05
Pedestrians at intersections must obey traffic signals: on red they do not cross, on yellow they must not start across, and on green they may cross, unless a pedestrian signal or officer directs otherwise. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec04-F27 | anchor: A05
A lit WALK sign or walking-person symbol lets pedestrians cross in the signal's direction, and the drivers of all vehicles must give them the right-of-way. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec04-F28 | anchor: A05
A flashing DON'T WALK or upraised hand with a countdown timer still lets pedestrians start, but they must finish crossing before the count reaches zero; without a countdown, a flashing hand means they may not start. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec04-F29 | anchor: A05
A steady DON'T WALK or upraised hand means no pedestrian may start crossing, and anyone already lawfully in the road must get to a curb, sidewalk, safety zone or other safe place as soon as possible. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec04-F30 | anchor: A06
Pavement markings are white or yellow, and broken white lines divide lanes moving the same way; stay inside your lane without straddling, and pass only when safe. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F31 | anchor: A06
A solid white line between same-direction lanes means no lane changes and no passing, and solid white also marks the highway edge and the line between a travel lane and the shoulder. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F32 | anchor: A06
Yellow lines divide traffic moving in opposite directions: a broken yellow line allows passing when safe, while a solid yellow line means do not cross or pass and also marks the left edge of multi-lane divided highways. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F33 | anchor: A06
With double yellow lines, you may not pass if the line on your side is solid. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F34 | anchor: A06
Always stop before a crosswalk, and at intersections where no crosswalk is painted you must still yield to pedestrians. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F35 | anchor: A06
A center left-turn lane, edged by solid and broken yellow lines, may be crossed only to turn left onto or off the highway and is never a travel or passing lane. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F36 | anchor: A06
You may drive no more than 200 feet in a center turn lane before turning left, and no more than 50 feet in it after turning onto the highway before merging (NRS 484B.223). [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F37 | anchor: A07
At a railroad crossing with a stop sign you must stop, and when a train is coming you must stop at least 15 feet from the tracks. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F38 | anchor: A07
Passenger buses and trucks hauling flammable or dangerous materials must stop at railroad crossings even when no signal shows and no train is coming. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F39 | anchor: A07
Never drive around a lowered crossing gate even if no train is visible, and when crossing lights flash you must stop and may go only if no train is visible or it is safe. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F40 | anchor: A07
Never park within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F41 | anchor: A07
Disobeying a school crossing guard is a misdemeanor in Nevada, and drivers must wait until the guard has fully left the crosswalk. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F42 | anchor: A07
School-zone speed limits are 15 or 25 mph and apply on school days from half an hour before classes start until half an hour after they end, unless posted otherwise; if flashing yellow lights are off during class time, the regular limit applies. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F43 | anchor: A07
U-turns in a school zone are banned except when no children are present, on days without school, outside the half-hour windows around the school day, or when signs or lights show the zone is not in effect. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0033]

Misconceptions: a flashing yellow arrow does not give you the right-of-way, oncoming traffic still goes first; a green arrow protects the turn but pedestrians in the crosswalk still have priority; a dark traffic light is a full stop, not a free pass; a left on red is legal only between two one-way streets; a yield sign does not require a full stop when the way is clear.
Mnemonics: octagon eight for stop, pentagon five for school; red stops, yellow warns, orange works, blue serves, brown plays; two hundred feet in, fifty feet out of the center lane; fifteen feet from the train, fifty feet to park.
Glossary: crossbuck means the X-shaped sign at the tracks themselves; stop line means the wide white line where you stop before the intersection; center turn lane means the shared middle lane used only for left turns; protected turn means a turn made on a green arrow with conflicting traffic held; regulatory sign means a sign stating a law you must obey.
Dynamic facts: posted school-zone hours, work-zone fine amounts and any locally signed exceptions vary by location; read the posted signs.

corpus_stability.reason: The Nevada Driver's Handbook carries one edition line on its cover (DMV 700 March 2024) and one copyright year on its title page, with a short key-changes list; nothing in the selected pages suggests more than one rewrite per year. The edition is about two and a half years old at intake, so currency is held as freshness debt in part A.
